results.title: Destiny Rings: Proximity-powered dating, social & networking
results.content:
There are three modes — Dating, Social, and Networking — so it's not just for romance. Whether you're trying to meet people at a happy hour, make friends in a new city, or connect with someone in your industry at a conference, the mechanic is the same: real proximity, real timing, real people.  
  
We're launching first in Hoboken, NJ before expanding to Jersey City and NYC. The app is live now (ring hardware is in final validation), so you can try Go Live mode today without a ring — proximity, Signals, and Fate Check all work through the app alone.  
  
Would love your feedback, especially on the onboarding flow and what would make this feel like a no-brainer to try at your next night out. Thanks for checking it out! 🙏 [...] Stella Reed

@destinyringsofficial That makes sense. The adjustable range sounds like a good way to handle different environments. I’m curious to see how it performs as more people start using it in real crowded places.

Gabe Labadie

This seems like a great product! How have you begun to launch this in the NYC area? When can we expect the first destiny marriage?

@gabe\_labadie We are starting with our in-app go-live mode while the rings are in production. Destiny marriage is the goal - not sure when but we'll leave it up to destiny!

Jessica Gonzalez [...] Destiny Rings
Destiny Rings

Destiny Rings

@stella\_reed1 Great question! In dense/crowded areas, the app uses signal strength and configurable detection range to filter out noise — so instead of pinging you about everyone within 100 feet at a packed bar, it prioritizes people who are genuinely close (a few feet away) and compatible based on your preferences. You can also adjust your detection range in settings if you want it tighter or wider depending on the environment. Still very much in beta and something we're actively tuning as we get more real-world usage data — appreciate you asking, this is exactly the kind of edge case we want to get right before scaling up!

Stella Reed

@dmitry\_petrakov Appreciate that “making the invisible legible” is exactly the intent.

In practice, we expect both behaviors. Early on, it acts like an inspection layer: users build intuition by seeing real signals on familiar sites. Over time, that awareness stabilizes into passive trust, where StealthHound runs quietly and only surfaces when something meaningfully deviates from a user’s baseline.

The UX goal is to avoid alert fatigue, it should fade into the background once it’s taught you how to see again.

Really like the idea of turning something invisible into something legible.

once users start seeing concrete "risk signals", does it change behavior over time – or does it mostly serve as an inspection / debugging tool?

In other words, do you see StealthHound as something people keep running passively, or something they dip into when they feel "something’s off"?

Congrats on the launch – performance-first + local-only is a strong stance 👏
